title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs help us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
claim: Model performance and narrative access vary systematically across query and target languages relative to English, leaving persistent gaps even when diversity is requested.
layout: 5 aligned panels left-to-right sharing a language row axis, diverging bars
description: A wide figure with five side-by-side horizontal bar panels (A–E) that share one y-axis listing 23 languages from Amharic to Urdu, with English as a hollow-diamond reference row. A legend on top shows Baseline Prompt in blue-gray, Diverse Prompt in purple, and green and red squares for the best and worst observed values. Panels A, B and D show language-minus-English gaps in percentage points as diverging bars, with dots and whiskers for confidence intervals. Panel B marks sparse estimates with daggers. Panel C uses tan bars for the framing gap. Panel E shows source-omission bars, mostly 25–65 pp. Bars point mostly left in B, C and D, which shows the shortfall relative to English. The eye goes to the green and red squares marking the extremes.
caption: Narrative access across languages relative to English. (A) Query-language performance across all five tasks. (B) Target narrative-language performance on narrative inclusion and exclusion. (C) Mean absolute BP/DP recall gap between neutral and confirmatory queries, by query language. (D) Narrative recall by query language under baseline prompting (BP) and diverse prompting (DP). (E) Source-language omission: the share of responses citing no document in an available source language. All panels show language-minus-English differences in percentage points; BP and DP use separate English baselines. Higher values mean better performance in A, B and D, larger framing gaps in C and more omissions in E. Whiskers show 95% intervals where available; daggers ($\dagger$) mark sparse target-language estimates without intervals. Green and red squares mark the best and worst observed values: smallest and largest absolute gaps in A--B, smallest and largest framing gaps in C, highest and lowest DP recall in D, and lowest and highest DP omission in E.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce \textsc{NarrativeBench}, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. \textsc{NarrativeBench} provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.
